Apart from the buzzing squadrons. Did you see Mrs. Higgins at the swings? She was giving me the side-eye again. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) Mrs. Higgins? Always has something to say, doesn't she? Probably thinks we’re abandoning Elsie to socialize. She's a lovely woman, in her own way, just… intense. Anyway, zapper it is. I'll order one tonight. Think we should go for the electric one or the CO2 lure thing? Speaker_1: CO2, definitely. More effective, I read. Though slightly more terrifying to imagine a horrifying, mosquito-attracting aura emanating from our patio. Still, preferable to Elsie looking like she's got the measles. What about that Florence + The Machine gig? Are you still keen on going next month? Speaker_2: Absolutely! I managed to snag some decent tickets, remember? Row G, surprisingly. I was bracing myself for being behind a giant speaker. We’ll have to sort out childcare. Mum and Dad are going to the theatre that weekend, aren’t they? Speaker_1: Yes, they mentioned that. I might be able to persuade Sarah to babysit. She’s been wanting to spend more time with Elsie, and she’s brilliant with her. Though, if we go, we’ll have to leave *before* the encore. My back is already starting to complain about pushing this buggy around for an hour. Speaker_2: Right, sensible. We don’t want you creaking like an old gate all week. Speaking of journeys, the traffic was absolutely bonkers on the way here. Sat on the A11 for almost twenty minutes. What was all that about? Roadworks again? Speaker_1: Probably. They're permanently doing some sort of repair on that road, aren't they? It's like it's *designed* to cause maximum disruption. I was thinking of taking the back roads next time, even if it does add another fifteen minutes. My nerves couldn't handle another twenty minutes of bumper-to-bumper frustration. Speaker_2: Good shout. The back roads are a bit more scenic, anyway. Though, you've got to watch out for tractors. Remember that time we got stuck behind that farmer and his combine harvester? Elsie found it hilarious, though. Speaker_1: (Laughing) She does love a tractor. Everything's a source of amusement for her at the moment. Have you looked at the course outlines for next semester yet? I’m starting to feel the pressure already. Professor Davies wants me to incorporate more digital humanities stuff. Speaker_2: Ugh, Davies. Always pushing boundaries. I’ve started, yeah. Lots of interdisciplinary nonsense, as usual. I'm trying to figure out how to make post-structuralism relevant to a class of undergraduates. It’s a challenge, to say the least. Speaker_1: Tell me about it. I’m thinking of using some interactive mapping software to explore Victorian social structures. It might…might… actually engage them. Speaker_2: That sounds genuinely interesting, actually. Could work well. At least it's better than another lecture on Foucault, which, let’s be honest, half of them would just switch off after five minutes. Speaker_1: Precisely! Although, I do think Foucault is rather brilliant. It’s finding the balance, isn’t it? Between intellectual rigor and… not sending them all running screaming. Speaker_2: (Nods) The eternal struggle of a lecturer. Right, Elsie’s starting to get a bit restless. Let's head back. I’ll pop to the shops on the way and grab some more of that mosquito repellent

Speaker_2: (Sighs dramatically, flopping onto the sofa next to Speaker_1) Honestly, this recruitment process is *killing* me. Another rejection email this morning. "While your skills are impressive…" blah, blah, blah. You know the drill. Speaker_1: (Putting down his golf clubs near the door, wincing slightly) Aye, I do. Rough, innit? Must be disheartening. Long day on the green, though. Nearly lost it on the 12th. Had a dodgy slice that ended up in the rough. Proper nightmare. Speaker_2: Rougher than a rejection email, I bet. Did you at least get some exercise? I feel like I’ve fossilised on this sofa. I barely left the flat today, except to chuck the post in the bin. Speaker_1: Loads. Swinging a club for five hours? That's a workout. You should try it, loosen you up a bit. Get you away from the phone. You're glued to it, you are. Speaker_2: Easy for you to say, Mr. Outdoor Athlete! I’m applying for jobs *on* the phone! And the computer. I need to be connected. Did you see that new theatre production they're doing at the Globe? "Wuthering Heights." Thinking of trying to get tickets. Need something to distract me. Speaker_1: Wuthering Heights? Sounds a bit… gloomy, doesn’t it? Bit too much brooding for me. I'd prefer something with a bit more… pep. Like that new sitcom on BBC, 'Up the Lift.' Proper laugh that. Speaker_2: (Chuckles) You and your sitcoms. You know, I was thinking, Halloween's coming up. Should we do anything? I’ve got that old ghost story anthology my gran gave me. Maybe we could have a spooky movie night? Speaker_1: Spooky? Blimey, you trying to scare me? I’m not a fan of all that ghost malarkey. Though, I did hear old Mrs. Higgins next door muttering about a spectral presence in her toilet again. Said she saw a shimmering… something. Speaker_2: (Laughing) Mrs. Higgins sees ghosts in her toilet. Classic. Maybe it’s just the plumbing. Probably needs some pipework. Remember when you had that leak last year? Drove us both mad. Speaker_1: Don't remind me. Cost a fortune. Anyway, have you thought about applying for that thing in Manchester? The recruitment agency mentioned it. It's with that tech firm. Speaker_2: Yeah, I have. It's a long shot, but it's worth a punt. The salary’s decent, and the company looks innovative. It’s just… so far away. I’d hate to move so far from home, even though Mum keeps subtly hinting I should "find my own place.” Speaker_1: Well, think of all the new songs you’d hear! Proper music scene in Manchester. And, you know, I could visit sometimes. It wouldn't be *that* bad, would it? More time practicing my putting, too. Speaker_2: (Leaning against him) You’re trying to bribe me with golf and new music. Very smooth, love. Honest, have you even thought about the future a bit? Like, beyond hitting golf balls and watching telly? Speaker_1: Of course I have! Just... less pressing than getting the next birdie, you know? I'm trying to get my game solid enough to hopefully qualify for the European Tour next year. That's the big goal. Proper serious stuff. Speaker_2: Tour, eh? Big stuff indeed! Still, even a successful golfer needs downtime. You need to relax, unwind. Right, I'm starving. Fancy ordering some Thai? I'm craving a green curry. Speaker_1: Sounds good to me. Thai’s always a winner. Should I get some more of that mango sticky rice? We always demolish it. Speaker_2: You read my mind! And maybe, if I’m lucky, after the curry and a bit

…and then the little green man landed right in the spaghetti! Wee! Wee! Wee!” Four-year-old Finn (Speaker_4) shrieked, clapping his hands, a smear of tomato sauce adorning his cheek. He was mid-song, a garbled, enthusiastic rendition of something vaguely space-related. Speaker_1 (Declan, the Irish IT manager): (chuckling, his accent thick and warm) “Ah, now, Finn, that’s a grand story, that is. A little green man in the spaghetti! Did he eat any?" Speaker_2 (Liam, the British student): “Sounds messy! Mum, did you see that documentary about space junk the other day? Apparently, there’s tonnes of it orbiting Earth. More than you'd think.” Speaker_3 (Sarah, the British woman caring for her toddler): “Liam, darling, please. Not space junk at dinner. Finn’s trying to sing, and I’m already exhausted. Honestly, this cloud computing stuff Declan’s been on about is giving me a headache.” She sighed, pushing a stray tendril of hair behind her ear. "It's just… baffling." Declan: "Now, Sarah, I was just explaining it was essential for the project at work. It’s not as complicated as it sounds. We're moving everything to the cloud, making it more accessible and secure. Think about it, you can access your photos from anywhere.” Liam: “Yeah, like backing stuff up. Remember when your hard drive crashed, Mum? Imagine if you’d had everything on the cloud then.” Sarah: "Yes, yes, I remember the heartbreak. All those pictures of your dad... But still, it feels like the whole world is relying on these massive, invisible servers floating around. It's unsettling, isn’t it?” Finn: (stopping his singing momentarily) “Servers! Big computers!” He pointed a sauce-covered finger at Declan. “Like yours, Daddy? Are there little green men on your computer too?” Declan: (laughing) “Not yet, Finn. Maybe one day! But for now, it’s just bits and bytes and code. Now, finish your pasta, champ. We’re having roast chicken tomorrow, you know.” Liam: "Roast chicken sounds good. Are we watching a film after? I was thinking of re-watching *Interstellar*. That cloud scene was pretty intense." Sarah: “*Interstellar*? Liam, honestly! Finn will have nightmares. Remember how scared he was during *Toy Story*?” Liam: “But it’s a classic! And the science is actually quite interesting.” Declan: "Right, let's not get bogged down in films just yet. I need to sort out arrangements for Uncle Seamus’s birthday next week. He’s turning seventy." Sarah: "Oh, Seamus! I forgot. Should we be getting him something? He's notoriously difficult to buy for.” Declan: "I was thinking of a voucher for that pub in Bandon. He loves a pint of Murphy’s and a bit of trad music." Liam: "Sounds perfect. I could help with organizing it all. Maybe get a banner? A big 'Happy 70th, Seamus!' one?" Sarah: “That’s a lovely idea, Liam. You’re good with those sorts of things.” She looked at Declan. "Are you sorting out the travel then? Seamus doesn't drive anymore." Declan: “Aye, I’m coordinating the carpools. Mary and Patrick are offering to give him a lift, but I need to check with them about the timings. It’s a bit of a logistical nightmare, to be honest.” He rubbed his temples. "Between work, Finn, and now Seamus's birthday, I'm completely swamped.” Finn: (begins singing again, louder this time) "Little green man, spaghetti land, zoom, zoom, zoom!" Sarah: “Oh, for goodness sake, Finn. A little quieter, please. My head is pounding.” She paused. "Declan, you really should take some time off. You’re working far too hard.” Declan

About the extension.” Speaker_1: "Oh, here we go. The extension. Don’t tell me you’ve got Pinterest boards going already. Are you picturing a ballroom or something?" Speaker_2: “Not a ballroom, silly. Though that *would* be lovely. I was thinking a proper kitchen, James. A proper one! With an island, and space for everyone. It's perfectly serviceable.” Speaker_2: “Perfectly serviceable isn’t the same as inspiring! I can’t create a delicious roast dinner when I'm practically tripping over the toaster. Somewhere to host Christmas properly, without people crammed into the living room.” Speaker_1: "Christmas…yes. That's a good point. Mum would appreciate a proper dining room. And Aunt Carol's awful fruitcake needs a dedicated staging area." Speaker_2: (Laughing) "Exactly! Practical considerations, James. You are a man of logic after all.” She nudged him playfully. "I was looking at some plans – a conservatory-style extension, blending in with the existing brickwork, lots of light..." Speaker_1: "Blending in is good. Don't want to stick out like a sore thumb. Although, a little bit of glass would be nice. Imagine being able to sit there in the winter, looking out at the snow..." Speaker_3: "Can we get a pet lion for the garden?" Speaker_2: (Smiling) "Absolutely not, darling. Lions are far too dangerous. How about a very fluffy cat?" Speaker_4: “A panther! A mini panther!” Speaker_1

Speaker_2: (Sipping his coffee, a slight frown on his face) Honestly, Idris, this coffee's a bit weak this morning. Reminds me of the water they give you in some budget hotels. Not quite the robust brew we deserve, is it? Speaker_1: (Adjusting his glasses, a hint of amusement in his voice) You're always complaining about the coffee, Rhys. It’s perfectly serviceable. Besides, I'm far more concerned about the funding application deadline looming. That Hadron Collider project proposal... are you making any progress on the supplementary data analysis? Speaker_2: (Waves a dismissive hand) Progress? Minimal, I’m afraid. The bloody grant committee are quibbling over the methodologies again. Said my suggestion of using fractal analysis was “too speculative.” Speculative! It’s revolutionary, Idris, revolutionary! They want something… pedestrian. Like counting particles. Can you believe it? Speaker_1: (Chuckles softly) They often do. They like to play it safe. But fractal analysis *is* rather elegant. Did you mention the potential for applying it to dark matter distribution? That’s the real selling point. Speaker_2: Of course I did! Repeatedly! They just… glazed over. It’s like talking to a wall. You know, this reminds me of trying to convince my wife, Bronwen, that we needed Tuscan terracotta tiles in the bathroom. Speaker_1: (Raises an eyebrow) Tuscan terracotta? Sounds rather… continental. Your wife strikes me as a woman of understated elegance, not Tuscan peasantry. Speaker_2: (Laughs heartily) Understated elegance? Idris, you haven't met her when she's wielding a power drill! Anyway, she argued for a simple white tile. "Practical," she said. “Easy to clean.” As if practicality is the sole measurement of artistic merit! I lost that battle, needless to say. We have white tiles. Speaker_1: (Smiling) Ah, the eternal struggle between academic creativity and domestic pragmatism. I’m familiar with that fight. My wife, Amelia, has been on a rampage decorating the downstairs loo. Wallpaper featuring flamingoes. Flamingos, Rhys! Speaker_2: (Gasps dramatically) Flamingos! In England? That’s… bold. Really bold. Speaker_1: Bold bordering on absurd, I'd say. I tried to subtly suggest something a little more subdued. Perhaps a nice William Morris pattern? She just gave me *the look*. You know the one. Speaker_2: Oh, I know that look. Keeps you in line, doesn't it? Speaking of travel, Amelia's flamingo aesthetic reminds me... Have you ever been to Italy, Idris? Properly been, I mean, not just for a conference. Speaker_1: Indeed, I have. Several times. Florence is breathtaking, of course, but I’ve always been partial to the Amalfi Coast. The lemon groves, the turquoise water… utterly divine. It’s a considerably better climate for contemplating the finer points of theoretical physics than Cairo, I can assure you. Speaker_2: You’re making me envious. Tredegar doesn’t exactly offer the same charm. Although, we do have some decent slate quarries, if you’re into that kind of gritty beauty. But I’d give anything for a week under the Italian sun right now. All this grant application stress…it’s exhausting. I've been wishing I'd invested in one of those fancy water filters, too. Ever noticed how much plastic is in bottled water these days? Feels like privatised rivers – these water companies, bleating on about essential services... Speaker_1: A perfectly valid complaint, Rhys. Corporate greed knows no bounds. I read a rather alarming report last week about… (trails off, distracted) Oh, bother. I almost forgot. I was just speaking to Professor Davies about his preliminary findings in the quantum entanglement project. He’s managed to achieve sustained entanglement for nearly a full second! Speaker_2: (Leans forward, eyes widening) A full second? Blimey! That's incredible. That drastically changes the modelling parameters for the Hadron Collider, doesn't it?

Speaker_1: (Sighs contentedly, surrounded by a colourful explosion of Lego bricks) Right, Operation Lego Sort is officially underway. Honestly, you two are brilliant at building, absolutely terrible at tidying. Look at this – a rogue Transformer amongst the Hogwarts castle! It's chaos! Speaker_2: (Age 6, bouncing on the bed) But Mummy, the Transformer was defending Hogwarts! From… from… a giant purple squid! Speaker_3: (Age 8, meticulously separating blue bricks into a pile) No, he wasn't, Maisie. Transformers fight Decepticons. Hogwarts is for wizards. It's basic Harry Potter lore. Speaker_3: (Without looking up from his pile) It's diluting the aesthetic. The castle needs a distinct colour palette. Think about it, Mummy, Gryffindor colours are red and gold. Right, while you two are being exceptionally organised, I was thinking… cinema this weekend? We could finally see that new Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles movie. Speaker_2: Ooh! Yes! Leo is my favourite! Does he get a new katana? Speaker_3: (Still sorting) It's a reboot. They’re probably changing everything. Probably making Michelangelo overly sensitive and Raph sarcastic for edgy appeal. Speaker_1: (Laughs) You've clearly done your research. Don’t worry, I'm sure they’ll be entertaining, even if they lose a bit of their original charm. Although, speaking of charm… are you two still obsessed with The Simpsons? Speaker_2: (Jumping off the bed) Yes! Bart is the best! He puts itching powder in Milhouse's pants! Speaker_3: (Quietly) Homer’s donut consumption is a fascinating study in behavioural economics. Speaker_1: (Shaking her head fondly) Where do you learn these things? Honestly, Finn. Right, well, while we’re in a reminiscing mood, Granny’s been on to me about those renovations she wants done. The kitchen needs a new floor, apparently. Speaker_2: Granny’s house is wobbly! Speaker_3: The foundation is showing signs of differential settling. It's probably a combination of soil erosion and poorly laid drainage. Speaker_1: (Rolling her eyes playfully) You’re certainly helpful. Are you two going to help me sort this Lego mountain, or are you going to become structural engineers? Speaker_2: Lego! Lego! Speaker_3: I can estimate the volume of bricks and suggest an optimised storage solution. We could utilise a modular shelving system… Speaker_1: (Interrupting) Right, hold that thought. Let’s just stick to colours for now, eh? And speaking of optimisation... have you two been sneaking Easter chocolate again? I swear, the bunny’s stash is disappearing at an alarming rate. Speaker_2: (Guilty smile) Maybe… just a little. Speaker_3: It’s a controlled experiment, Mummy. We’re testing the rate of cocoa bean degradation under room temperature. For science. Speaker_1: (Laughing) “For science!” You are unbelievable. Okay, scientists, back to Lego. Blue bricks, people! And then, maybe, *maybe*, we can discuss the finer points of chocolate decomposition. But no more sneaking until after dinner, understood? Speaker_2: Understood! Speaker_3: Affirmative. Though I hypothesize that a carefully controlled refrigeration regime could significantly extend its… (Speaker_1 cuts him off with a playful shushing sound).

Speaker_2: (Slamming the fridge door a little too hard) Honestly, this fridge is practically empty! You've been gone a week, Liv, and you’d think I’d been single-handedly feeding an army. Speaker_1: (Smiling, kicking off her shoes by the door) Sorry! Didn't realise. Holidays do strange things to a person's appetite, you know? Mostly I just lived off croissants and vaguely suspicious-looking pastries. Speaking of which, feeling hungry now. Are you making dinner? Speaker_2: Potentially. Depends if you’re contributing. I was thinking pasta, but I’m low on everything. How was Greece, by the way? Seriously, tell me everything. You were practically non-existent on WhatsApp. Speaker_1: It was… amazing! Really amazing. Such different vibes to anything I've experienced before. The beaches were postcard perfect, obviously, but it was the people, the energy... it kind of shifted something in me, I think. I actually, unexpectedly, met someone. Speaker_2: (Eyes widening) You met someone?! Liv! Don’t tell me you’ve brought back a ridiculously handsome Greek god! Spill! What’s he like? Photos! I demand photos! Speaker_1: (Laughing) Hold your horses! He’s not a Greek god, more like... a very charming fisherman. His name’s Dimitri, and he runs a little boat tour. He showed me the best hidden coves, cooked me the freshest seafood... It was really lovely. No photos yet, though. Still pretty early days, you know? Speaker_2: Early days? You’re back already! You’ve barely unpacked! I bet he cried when you left. A fisherman with a broken heart… tragic. So, tell me everything! Was he tall? Dark hair? Did he serenade you with a bouzouki? Speaker_1: (Rolling her eyes playfully) He's definitely tall, dark hair, and surprisingly good with a bouzouki, yes! He did give me a little knitted octopus as a farewell gift, which was… sweet. It's a bit cheesy, but in the best way. I'm thinking of going back in a couple of months. Speaker_2: A couple of months? Wow! That's serious. You're going to need a proper plan then. Flights, accommodation... Did you even think about the time difference? And what about work? I mean, you just landed this Project Co-ordinator role, don't you want to stick with it? Speaker_1: I know, I know. It’s all a bit… chaotic, to be honest. But it felt right while I was there. And I do like my job, truly. It's just... Dimitri makes it feel like there's more out there than spreadsheets and client meetings. Anyway, back to you! How was the ward? Anything interesting happen while I was away? Speaker_2: Interesting? Let’s just say I’ve seen things. One patient was convinced he was a potato. A very dramatic potato. We had to convince him he wasn't, which took most of a Tuesday. And Sarah's off sick, so I've been covering her shifts. It’s exhausting. I really need a holiday. Speaker_1: Oh no, a potato! That's… intense. Sorry to hear about Sarah, and you covering her shifts. You deserve a medal, seriously. Listen, can I just ask – did Mum call while I was gone? I tried ringing her a couple of times, but got no answer. Speaker_2: Yeah, she did. She called three times! She’s worried sick about you, as always. Apparently, she was grilling Aunt Carol about whether you were eating properly. She sent me a picture of a shepherd's pie. A perfectly formed, very beige shepherd's pie. Speaker_1: (Groaning) Oh, Mum. You know she does that. Honestly, the shepherd's pie is just a weapon. She’s trying to guilt me into coming home more often. Which, you know, I *want* to do, but... Greece is tempting.

In this weather? It's far too damp for roses. They’ll get mildew. Speaker_1: (Exasperated) Arthur, the roses were taking over *last* week, in slightly damp weather!
